claim: Hindenburg and Ludendorff, at Ober Ost from 1 November, were asking for reinforcements in the east.
Przemyśl fell with its garrison in March 1915 and Conrad told Berlin the Carpathian front could not be held without German help; Falkenhayn feared a separate peace.
note: Falkenhayn's fear is stated as his, not Conrad's threat.

claim: Hindenburg and Ludendorff proposed a wide envelopment of the Russian armies in Poland out of East Prussia and Courland; Falkenhayn rejected it.
Mackensen's Eleventh Army opened the Gorlice-Tarnow offensive on 2 May 1915.
By the end of the summer Russia had lost Poland and part of the Baltic provinces without its armies being destroyed.
note: Great Retreat.

claim: Bulgaria signed a military convention with the Central Powers on 6 September 1915 putting German, Austro-Hungarian and Bulgarian armies under Mackensen against Serbia.
note: The date, 6 September 1915, is confirmed (24 August is the Old Style date that some sources give). The arrangement putting the armies under Mackensen was not checked in this pass, so the claim stays drafted.

claim: The attack opened in early October; Belgrade fell within days; the Serbian army retreated through Albania in winter; a rail link to Constantinople opened by about the new year.
note: Check the date the through rail link first carried German supplies (late 1915 to early 1916).

claim: Serbia had turned back three Austro-Hungarian invasions in 1914.
The British and French attacked on the Somme on 1 July 1916; the line held at most points but not at the southern end.
A standing order that no ground was to be given up and lost ground retaken at once governed the German defence of the Somme in July 1916.
note: Sources differ on who issued it: it is attributed to Falkenhayn, and also to Second Army (Below, 3 July) after Falkenhayn dismissed Second Army's chief of staff, Grunert, for ordering a withdrawal. The node puts the rule as a decision for the Chief and says only that the order went to Second Army in the first days of July.

claim: The order led to piecemeal counter-attacks at heavy cost.
note: A common judgment; cite a source.

claim: The Hindenburg Programme was set out at the end of August 1916 and aimed to double munitions output and triple the supply of guns and machine guns by spring 1917.
note: The exact date (31 August is often given) and the machine-gun figure were not confirmed in the web pass; the node now says the end of August.

claim: The Auxiliary Service Law passed the Reichstag in December 1916 with amendments the Supreme Command did not want.
note: The law is dated 5 December 1916; the date of its passage through the Reichstag was not confirmed, so the node says December.

claim: The winter of 1916-17 brought a failed potato harvest, a coal shortage and railway breakdown (the turnip winter).
The Kaiser ordered the withdrawal to the Hindenburg (Siegfried) Line on 4 February 1917, with the intervening ground to be devastated; the retirement began on 9 February.
note: Main movement 16-19 March.

claim: The new line was about 40-45 km shorter and needed 13-14 fewer divisions.

claim: Rupprecht's army group asked for the withdrawal over the objections of the First and Second Army commanders, and Ludendorff accepted it reluctantly. Kuhl, Rupprecht's chief of staff, advocated it.
Roads were mined, wells fouled, villages burned, orchards cut and civilians removed; the destruction damaged German prestige in neutral countries.
note: Check 'wells fouled' wording against a specialist source.

claim: Rupprecht supported the withdrawal but objected to the devastation, on the ground that it damaged the Empire's prestige and the discipline of the troops.
note: A characterization of his recorded objection. Corrected from the drafted version, which said he argued it harmed Germany's name abroad more than the enemy; the sources give prestige and discipline. The node's wording now follows.

claim: Austria-Hungary asked Germany for help after eleven Isonzo battles; Ludendorff judged six to eight divisions could be spared; a Fourteenth Army of German and Austro-Hungarian divisions under Otto von Below attacked on 24 October 1917.
note: Sources differ on the exact number of German divisions (six or seven); the text gives a range.

claim: The Italians retreated to the Piave and the Allies sent divisions to hold them.

claim: A crown council at Bad Homburg on 13 February 1918, with the Kaiser, Hertling, Kühlmann, Hindenburg, Ludendorff and Hoffmann present, decided to resume the advance.
The advance began on 18 February; Minsk fell on the 21st and Kiev on 2 March; Russia signed on 3 March.
Kühlmann doubted the military's eastern programme, and held that Russia would have to be part of a European settlement and that Brest-Litovsk was a temporary arrangement.
note: Characterization; the node's wording is indirect speech.

claim: Blücher-Yorck was planned as a diversion to draw Allied reserves from Flanders, ahead of Hagen.
The attack began 27 May, crossed the Vesle (where the plan said to stop), took Soissons on 29 May and reached the Marne on 30 May.
OHL drew divisions held for Hagen into the Blücher fight; Hagen was repeatedly put off and not carried out.

On 8 August 1918 British, Australian and Canadian troops attacked east of Amiens with tanks and aircraft; some German divisions did not fight; thousands were taken prisoner; Ludendorff called it the black day of the German army.
A council at Spa on 14 August with the Kaiser, Hintze, Hindenburg and Ludendorff accepted a strategic defensive and asked Hintze to sound out peace through neutral channels.
Hintze's position is characterized as: a defensive must be joined to a diplomatic approach.
note: Characterization, not a quotation.

claim: Prince Max of Baden became Chancellor on 3 October and the request went out in the first week of October; Wilson replied on 8, 14 and 23 October.
Ludendorff, who asked for an armistice on 29 September, came to oppose the terms after the later notes.

The army order of 24 (some accounts 25) October was sent without the Chancellor's knowledge; he demanded Ludendorff's dismissal; on 26 October the Kaiser accepted Ludendorff's resignation, kept Hindenburg and named Groener.

claim: The Verdun attack was set for 12 February and put off by the weather; the bombardment began at 7.15 on 21 February and lasted about ten hours, and the infantry attacked at 4 in the afternoon.
About 1,201 guns (two-thirds of them heavy) were massed, 808 of them in the opening bombardment, firing about a million shells on the first day, with 2,000,000 planned for the first six days.

III Corps, VII Reserve Corps and XVIII Corps led the attack, each reinforced with 2,400 experienced troops and 2,000 recruits, with XV Corps in army reserve and Rohr's Sturm-Bataillon Number 5 in support.
On 25 February men of the Brandenburg Regiment 24 entered Fort Douaumont, held by a skeleton garrison of about 25 under Chenot, its guns having been removed in 1915.
Falkenhayn wanted the Meuse Heights and the French army bled; the Fifth Army staff's phrase 'relentless pressure' made the aim ambiguous.
The west-bank attack began on 6 March against the Mort-Homme and Hill 265 (Cote 265); German casualties to the end of March were 81,607.
The effectiveness weights of the arms and the setups' modifiers are game judgments, not measurements.
note: 62-battles.jsx.

claim: The March 1918 offensive used 74 divisions (44 of them 'mobile'), 6,600 guns, 3,500 mortars and 326 aircraft.

Hutier's Eighteenth Army, with about 27 divisions on both sides of St Quentin, was the only army to reach its first-day objectives; Below's Seventeenth Army was to attack toward Arras and Marwitz's Second along the Somme toward Amiens.
The bombardment opened at 4.35 and the barrage at 4.40 along a front of about 69 km, with more than 3.5 million shells in five hours; the infantry attacked at 9.40 in fog.

A directive of 23 March re-aimed the offensive at separating the British and French and then taking Amiens; Operation Mars on 28 March (29 divisions) was repulsed, and Ludendorff ended the offensive on 5 April; the gain was about 3,100 square kilometres, up to 65 km deep.
The effectiveness weights of the arms and the setups' modifiers are game judgments, not measurements.
note: 62-battles.jsx.

note: Widely reported; to be checked against Moltke's own account and Tuchman, Barbara, The Guns of August.

claim: The German potato harvest of 1916 failed and swedes (turnips) replaced potatoes in the diet of the cities in the winter of 1916 to 1917; bread, meat, fat and coal were rationed.
The winter of 1916 to 1917 is remembered in Germany as one of the hardest of the war for the home front (the Turnip Winter).
note: Corrected from 'the worst'; sources say one of the harshest. The coal and railway detail in the potato-failure claim was not confirmed by the pages read.

claim: On the afternoon of 1 August 1914 a telegram from the German ambassador in London reported that Britain would keep France out of the war if Germany did not attack her; the Kaiser took it as good news and asked Moltke whether the army could be deployed in the east only.

Moltke refused, saying that a deployment of that size could not be improvised; the Kaiser said that Moltke's uncle would have given a different answer, and accepted the argument; later that evening King George V sent word that the ambassador must have misunderstood.
note: The wording of the exchange differs between accounts; the node gives it in indirect speech.

claim: The head of the railway division, Hermann von Staab, argued after the war that the army could have been turned east at a day's notice; the General Staff had a plan for deploying against Russia alone, revised each year until 1913. Moltke held that it could not be done.

claim: Mobilisation had been ordered on 1 August and the Chief of the General Staff was carrying the signed order when the Kaiser recalled him.

The German attack of 11 November 1914 was made by twelve and a half divisions in two army groups, Fabeck's and Linsingen's, under Crown Prince Rupprecht, on a front of nine miles from Messines to Reutel.
The spearhead was the Prussian Guard and the 4th Division, about 10,000 men in twelve fresh battalions, against eleven tired British battalions of about 4,000 men.
note: Sources differ on the British numbers.

claim: The attack was preceded by a heavy bombardment and went in under morning mist; British artillery isolated the Guards from reinforcements, a gap north of the Menin Road was closed by counter-attacks, and by the afternoon a counter-attack had cleared the wood.
The reserve corps raised since August had gone in in mass at Langemarck in October and lost heavily for little ground.

claim: Epilogue, 'What actually happened': Bethmann Hollweg was forced out in July 1917, in the crisis over the Reichstag's peace resolution, at the insistence of the Supreme Command, and the governments that followed were weaker. Prince Max of Baden became Chancellor on 3 October 1918 and the request to President Wilson went out in the first days of that month. The armistice was signed on 11 November, and within a year the account of an army betrayed at home was in print.
note: Written in the endings pass from facts logged for the record endings and the reports; to be checked against a source before release.

claim: Epilogue, 'What actually happened': the United States declared war on Germany on 6 April 1917, after the resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare, and American divisions were in the line in France in the spring of 1918. The German request of October 1918 went to the President as the leader of an enemy, who answered it three times and set conditions that included the end of the monarchy's power and terms that left Germany unable to renew the war.
note: Written in the endings pass from facts logged for the record endings and the reports; to be checked against a source before release.

claim:
Epilogue, 'What actually happened': Austria-Hungary asked for an armistice at the end of October 1918, after the Italian victory at Vittorio Veneto, and it was signed at the Villa Giusti on 3 November, to take effect the next day. The monarchy dissolved into its successor states in the following weeks, and Germany signed its own armistice a week after the Austrian one.

In the real days that followed, the German staff did look at the open southern frontier, and Bavarian officers feared an Allied advance from Austria. In this ending the fear comes first and the armistice comes second, and the Supreme Command is asked which of its two frontiers it means to cover.
note: Written in the endings pass from facts logged for the record endings and the reports; to be checked against a source before release.

claim: Epilogue, 'What actually happened': Brest-Litovsk was signed on 3 March 1918, the German advance in the east took Kiev on 2 March, and the spring offensive in the west took ground and was stopped short of Amiens. The armistice of 11 November annulled the treaty and called for the withdrawal of German troops from the former Russian territories when the Allies judged the moment suitable.
note: Written in the endings pass from facts logged for the record endings and the reports; to be checked against a source before release.
